headline: Benjamin Ash, Ryotatsu Yanagimoto and Mandar Sohoni made the quasi-phase-matching grating inside a silicon-nitride waveguide a projected image rather than an etched structure, so the phase mismatch a fabrication error leaves behind can be corrected on the finished chip in about a second.

items.title: Project light on the electrodes and the phase matching becomes a setting
items.dek: Benjamin Ash, Ryotatsu Yanagimoto, Mandar Sohoni and co-authors made a silicon-nitride optical waveguide's second-order nonlinearity — the property that lets one wavelength of light generate another — programmable, by projecting a 532 nm pattern onto photoconductive electrodes so the phase-matching grating is written optically after the chip is fabricated.
items.why_it_matters: Phase matching in a nonlinear waveguide is normally etched or poled in at fabrication, so a few nanometres of width error anywhere along a centimetres-long device destroys the conversion and the die is scrap. Making the grating a projected image lets the mismatch be measured and cancelled in a closed loop on the finished part, which converts a yield loss into a calibration step.
items.background_md: Nonlinear optics needs two waves to stay in step. A waveguide that turns light of one wavelength into light at twice the frequency only accumulates signal if the two travel at the same phase velocity, and in any real material they do not: dispersion walks them out of step within a fraction of a millimetre. The standard fix is quasi-phase matching — reverse the sign of the material's second-order nonlinearity every coherence length so the error resets instead of accumulating. In ferroelectrics that reversal is frozen in by poling electrodes at fabrication time.
items.deeper_md:
Silicon nitride has no native χ⁽²⁾, so the grating is induced: a bias field turns the material's third-order response into an effective second-order one, `χ⁽²⁾(x,z) = 3χ⁽³⁾E_bias(x,z)`. The stack is a 2 µm PECVD nitride waveguide under a 9 µm silicon-rich-nitride photoconductive layer with a sputtered ITO top electrode, driven at 800 V AC at 10 Hz; a 532 nm image from a spatial light modulator decides where the field lands, at 3.8 µm spatial resolution.

The resulting χ⁽²⁾ is about 0.29 pm/V, and that is the weakness the authors name themselves, along with propagation loss capping how far efficiency scales, a ~1 Hz update rate set by the modulator, and a bench full of free-space optics. What it buys is reach: closed-loop optimisation compensated the mismatch in width-modulated and spiral waveguides, including 10.1 cm of propagation folded into 4.3 × 4.3 mm.

The competing route writes the same grating with no external field at all — the photogalvanic effect self-organises a χ⁽²⁾ pattern in nitride microresonators and reaches milliwatt on-chip second-harmonic power — but self-organised gratings are not independently addressable. A companion paper in the same announcement batch argues the diagnostic half matters more: sum-frequency tomography separates dispersion orders from longitudinal phase-mismatch variation and characterises a waveguide in seconds.

glossary.definition: The coefficient that says how strongly a material mixes two light fields into a third; it vanishes in any centrosymmetric material, which is why nitride and silicon need a trick to have one at all.

Periodically reversing the sign of χ⁽²⁾ along a waveguide so the phase error between the two waves is reset each coherence length instead of growing, which lets conversion accumulate over centimetres.
Using a static bias field plus the material's third-order nonlinearity to synthesise an effective χ⁽²⁾ where none exists naturally; the induced value scales linearly with the applied field.
A high-resistance layer that only conducts where light falls on it, so an optical image decides the voltage pattern reaching the device beneath instead of a fixed metal geometry.

items.fab_angle: The in-situ diagnostics are the transferable part: the same programmable field lets the authors read the dispersion of individual transverse modes and do on-chip wavefront phase tomography, which is linewidth and sidewall uniformity measured optically on a finished die rather than inferred from a CD-SEM on a monitor wafer.

items.title: Drop the resonator from a photonic memory and the calibration goes with it
items.dek: Ankur Singh and Akhilesh Jaiswal propose an optical memory cell built in GlobalFoundries' 45 nm silicon-photonics process out of variable optical attenuators instead of ring resonators, so the cell holds a bit with no wavelength tuning at all — and the layout for that one bit covers 147.92 × 219.93 µm².
items.why_it_matters: Every resonant photonic memory has to be tuned onto its cavity resonance and then held there against temperature drift, which is the reason none of them has scaled into an array. Take the resonance out and the tuning goes with it, and what is left standing is the honest bill for storing a bit in light: 0.562 pJ to write it, 50 µW of optical power to keep it, and 0.0325 mm² of die.
items.background_md: A memory cell holds a bit because two inverters feed each other: each output is the other's input, so the pair has two stable states and stays in whichever one it was pushed into. Photonic memories try to build the same loop out of light, and the usual ingredient is a microring resonator, whose transmission flips sharply as the wavelength crosses resonance. The sharpness is both the attraction and the problem — a resonance picometres wide has to be held on wavelength against fabrication spread and against every degree of temperature change.
items.deeper_md:
The cell is two attenuators, V1 and V2, each fed by a photodiode branch and an electrical buffer. The stored bit is the voltage difference between nodes Q and Q̄, and those voltages set how much light each attenuator passes; an optical write pulse unbalances the photocurrents, and the feedback drives the pair into the complementary state and holds it.

Numbers, all from circuit simulation in the 45SPCLO process design kit rather than from silicon: a 10 ps write pulse at 2 mW peak is 20 fJ incident, 100 fJ referred back to the laser at 20% wall-plug efficiency, on top of 461.6 fJ of electrical switching, for 0.562 pJ total. Holding costs 50 µW of optical input continuously. Retention was simulated for 5 s per state with no drift at measurement resolution, and the footprint is about 32.5% of a comparable microring latch.

The caveats are the authors': read extinction ratio is only 2.18 dB, the access attenuators' residual transmission has to stay under the write-disturb threshold, and array scaling still faces optical distribution loss and device variation. Non-volatile routes exist — a memristor on a microring switches in 300 ps at 0.15 pJ and retains for 12 hours — but need heterogeneous III-V integration, and the paper is explicit that comparing volatile with non-volatile means nothing until hold energy and retention are counted together.

glossary.definition: A waveguide section whose transmission is set electrically without relying on a cavity resonance, so its response is broad in wavelength and does not need tuning to a particular line.

The power ratio between the bright and dark states of an optical signal; 2.18 dB means the two stored states differ by under a factor of two in transmitted power, which is a thin margin for a receiver.
Optical power out of a laser divided by electrical power in; it is why an optical energy budget must be multiplied up before it is compared with an electrical one.
The foundry-supplied library of verified device models, layout rules and standard components that bounds what a designer is allowed to build on a given process.

items.title: A hydrogen plasma every cycle, and ALD titanium nitride grows ordered
items.dek: A group led by Yi-Hsun Chen inserted a hydrogen plasma step into every atomic-layer-deposition cycle and grew titanium nitride — the metal nitride already used as a gate metal and diffusion barrier in CMOS — as a semi-coherent epitaxial film on sapphire that superconducts at 2.2 K.
items.why_it_matters: Atomic layer deposition lays down a conformal film one fraction of a monolayer per cycle, but each cycle also strands fragments of the molecule the metal arrived in, and in a superconductor that residue is the disorder that sets the loss. Clearing it inside every cycle, rather than annealing at the end, is what let the lattice follow the substrate — so the knob that buys structural order is per-cycle surface chemistry, not a hotter deposition.
items.background_md: Atomic layer deposition builds a film from two self-limiting surface reactions run in alternation: one precursor saturates the surface and then stops, the chamber is purged, and a second reagent converts what stuck. A cycle adds a fixed fraction of a monolayer, so thickness is counted in cycles rather than timed, and the film coats the inside of a deep hole as faithfully as a flat top. What the technique does not normally deliver is a single crystal — each layer nucleates wherever it lands, so the result is polycrystalline or amorphous.
items.deeper_md:
Synchrotron X-ray scattering shows semi-coherent epitaxy of the nitride on c-plane sapphire with discrete crystallographic domains and little long-range structural disorder; X-ray spectroscopy and neutron reflectometry find negligible oxygen-related disorder through the thickness and no substantial hydrogen left behind by the plasma. The electrical result is a transition at 2.2 K, a sheet kinetic inductance of 15 pH/sq, and a superconducting coherence length of 14.6 nm — close enough to the measured crystal coherence length that the two are comparable.

The honest comparison is unflattering on T_c. Plasma-enhanced ALD titanium nitride with a substrate-bias densification step already reaches 4.35 K at roughly 40 nm while holding sheet resistance to within 95% uniformity across a 6-inch wafer, which is what reactive sputtering also gives. So the claim here is structural order and interface quality, not a better superconductor. Nor is 15 pH/sq in the regime ALD nitride is usually wanted for: an earlier ALD study reached 234 pH/sq with resonator quality factors of 0.4 to 1.0 million, and those were limited by two-level systems in the surrounding dielectric rather than by the metal.

Nobody disputes the diffraction. What the paper does not measure is whether the ordered film actually buys resonator quality factor, which is the number the application cares about.

glossary.definition: Inductance arising from the inertia of the superconducting carriers rather than from magnetic field geometry; it rises as a film gets thinner or more disordered, and it is why thin nitrides are used to make compact high-impedance circuits.
The distance over which the superconducting state cannot change abruptly; when it is comparable to the grain size, grain boundaries start to dominate the electrical behaviour of the film.
A surface reaction that stops once the surface is saturated, regardless of how much more precursor is supplied — the property that makes ALD thickness a count of cycles instead of a timed exposure.
The temperature below which a material's DC resistance goes to zero; for a thin film it falls with disorder and with thickness, so it doubles as a proxy for film quality.

items.fab_angle: Titanium nitride is already in a CMOS flow twice over, as a work-function metal in the gate stack and as the barrier that keeps copper out of silicon, and both uses are conformality problems solved by ALD. A plasma treatment inside each cycle is a recipe change rather than a tool change, which makes it the kind of knob a teaching fab with a plasma-capable ALD head can actually turn and measure with a four-point probe.

items.title: Nine domain walls per micron, and the terahertz output goes up fourfold
items.dek: Zeinab Abdul Hadi, Vincent Juvé and co-authors compared epitaxial bismuth ferrite films grown with different ferroelectric domain patterns and found the striped film — nine domain walls per micron — radiates a terahertz field four times stronger than the same material grown as a single domain.
items.why_it_matters: Why the stripes win settles an argument about which photocurrent makes the radiation: not the bulk photovoltaic shift current, but the ultrafast screening of the polarisation by photocarriers, sped up by the incompletely compensated bound charge sitting at every wall. That turns the domain configuration into a design parameter with a number attached to it, instead of a defect population to be annealed away.
items.background_md: A ferroelectric carries a built-in electric polarisation that persists with no applied field, and a thin film of one breaks into domains pointing different ways to lower its energy. The boundary between two domains is a wall a few unit cells thick, and because the polarisation changes across it, bound charge that the surrounding material only partly screens sits there — which means a local field far larger than any external electrode could impose. Whether those walls help a device or ruin it has been argued both ways for two decades.
items.deeper_md:
Four samples, each a different domain state: 180 nm on SrTiO₃(110) with an oblique single-domain polarisation, 125 nm on DyScO₃(011) polarised out of plane, 100 nm on DyScO₃(110) in periodic stripes at 9 domain walls µm⁻¹, and a 20 nm disordered mosaic. All were pumped at 400 nm, above the 2.7 eV gap, with 35 fs pulses at 1 kHz and about 0.5 mJ/cm².

The separation of mechanisms is the real result, and it comes from symmetry rather than from magnitude: resolving the emitted field in amplitude and phase against both pump polarisation and crystal orientation isolates a pump-polarisation-independent current, the screening term ∂P/∂t, from the bulk photovoltaic current that dominates only in the out-of-plane film. In the stripe and mosaic films the walls raise photocarrier density locally and separate charge in their own built-in fields, which accelerates screening.

Caveats the authors state: their maximum fluence was set by the setup, not the sample, so the stripe film's true saturation was never reached; detection covers only 0.2–3 THz; substrate birefringence splits the pump into copies delayed by 132 fs and 80 fs, needing spectral correction. The "half a spintronic emitter" benchmark is also a moving target — a CoFeB/Pt₇₅Au₂₅ alloy bilayer reported in APL in February puts out 30% more terahertz power than CoFeB/Pt.

glossary.definition: The few-unit-cell boundary where a ferroelectric's polarisation direction changes; uncompensated bound charge there produces a local electric field much stronger than an external bias can supply.
A photocurrent that flows in a material with no inversion symmetry without any junction or applied bias, set by the crystal's own symmetry rather than by a built-in field.

The transient current that flows when photogenerated carriers rush to cancel a ferroelectric's polarisation; because it is a rate of change of polarisation it radiates, and its direction is fixed by the crystal, not by the light.
Optical energy per unit area in a single pulse; emitters are compared at matched fluence because almost every mechanism saturates as it rises.

items.title: Schedule the recurrence first, and the CGRA's control words fold up
items.dek: Jun Yin and co-authors rebuilt how loops are scheduled onto a coarse-grained reconfigurable array — a mesh of small ALUs that changes function every cycle from a stored control word — by letting whichever timing constraint dominates shape the dataflow graph, and measured 2.18× the throughput of existing mappers.
items.why_it_matters: Two different things cap a loop's rate on this hardware: a value one iteration computes that the next iteration needs, and a compute node that takes several cycles to answer. Handling them in one pass instead of two makes the per-iteration offsets uniform, and uniform offsets let the emitted control sequence repeat on a shorter cycle than the initiation interval — 46% shorter — which also shrinks the configuration words that must be fetched.
items.background_md: A coarse-grained reconfigurable array is a grid of small arithmetic units with a programmable network between them, reconfigured every cycle from a stored control word. It sits between a CPU, which fetches an instruction per operation, and fixed-function hardware, which fetches none: the array pays for configuration memory and gets spatial parallelism without a new tapeout per kernel. Its compilation problem is modulo scheduling — assign every operation a phase such that a fresh loop iteration can start every II cycles, where the initiation interval II is the quantity being minimised.
items.deeper_md:
The target is a 4×4 multi-context mesh, with an 8×8 configuration for scaling, each tile carrying a SIMD compute unit, local and mesh FIFOs, a crossbar and an instruction buffer. Baselines are a vanilla OpenCGRA mapper, a PICACHU-like mapper with multi-cycle pipelining only, and a COMPOSE-like mapper with recurrence awareness only — so the comparison isolates doing both at once.

Ten kernels in three classes: loop-carried and multi-cycle (IIR biquad, LogSumExp, FlashAttention, MambaSSM), low-latency bitwise (Viterbi, dithering, TinyDES), and multi-cycle feed-forward (FFT, GeLU, SwiGLU). Results are 2.18× throughput, a 46% shorter emitted initiation interval, control-word overhead down 64% unrolled once and 44% unrolled four times, and 5.07× faster mapper convergence on the same heuristic backend.

The mechanism is that in multi-context modulo scheduling, operations, routes and buffered values all occupy hardware slots at particular modulo phases, so successive iterations overlap across configuration contexts; when the loop-carried offsets come out regular, the control stream itself repeats sooner than II. The caveat is the authors': the backend heuristic is incomplete and maps sequentially, so it has to try several candidates and II can rise when the first attempt fails. Exact alternatives exist — a SAT formulation of modulo scheduling beat prior mappers on roughly half its benchmarks — so completeness against speed is still an open trade.

glossary.definition: The number of cycles between the starts of successive loop iterations on a pipelined or spatially mapped loop; throughput is one iteration per II, so minimising it is the whole objective.
Scheduling a loop body so that each operation's cycle, taken modulo II, names a hardware slot nobody else is using, which is what lets iterations overlap in steady state.
A dependence from one iteration to the next — this iteration needs a value the previous one produced — which puts a hard floor under II that no amount of extra hardware removes.
One stored control word describing the whole array's function for a cycle; a multi-context array holds several and cycles between them, so configuration memory is traded against flexibility.

items.fab_angle: A reconfigurable array is the shape of accelerator a group with one tapeout can afford, because the kernel changes in software afterwards rather than in a new mask set — but the trade is explicit here, and it is configuration memory: control words are fetched every cycle, so the SRAM and the instruction-fetch bandwidth are part of the design, not an afterthought.

items.title: One wrong gcd in a rational divide, and the noise stops being Laplace
items.dek: Cesare Gerolimetto Fabrello and co-authors traced periodic ripples in the noise that OpenDP — the differential-privacy library used to publish statistics without exposing the individuals behind them — adds to query answers back to a division bug in a third-party Rust rational-arithmetic crate, not to the privacy mathematics.
items.why_it_matters: The reason this sampler is built from exact fractions in the first place is that floating point spaces its representable values unevenly, and those gaps leak which record was in the dataset. Rationals only buy that back if the rational arithmetic is right: a division that reduced by the wrong greatest common divisor skewed every Bernoulli coin flip slightly, and the reconstructed privacy-loss variable then steps outside the e^±ε bound the library promises.
items.background_md: Differential privacy makes a statistic safe to publish by adding noise calibrated to how much one person's record could move the answer; the guarantee is that no output becomes more than e^ε times likelier because you were in the data. That guarantee is a claim about an exact distribution, and a finite computer cannot draw from one — so implementations build the discrete Laplace and discrete Gaussian out of integer and rational arithmetic, composing biased coin flips with probabilities like e^{−x}, instead of rounding a floating-point sample.
items.deeper_md:
The fault is in `dashu`'s rational crate at v0.4, released January 2024, and reaches OpenDP v0.14.0 and earlier. Dividing `x = a/b` by an integer `k`, it formed the denominator as `(b/g)·k` rather than the correct `b·(k/g)` with `g = gcd(a, k)`. That matters because `bernoulli_exp1`, which draws Bernoulli(e^{−x}) for x in [0,1] and is called repeatedly by the discrete Laplace sampler, requests its probabilities through exactly that division — so every coin flip came back slightly wrong.

The signature is evenly spaced spikes and holes in the output histogram, symmetric about zero, with a spacing that depends on the Laplace scale; the main run used ε = 0.1, hence scale b = 10. Against the theoretical distribution the faulty primitive sits at z ≈ 11.3 with p ≈ 0 over 10⁶ samples, and the exact-rational replacement lands at z ≈ 1.8, p ≈ 0.07.

What is shown and what is not: they reconstruct the privacy-loss random variable and observe it crossing the e^±ε bound, which is empirical evidence of a broken guarantee rather than a proof of how much ε actually inflated, and no attack is presented. Nobody disputes the construction — Canonne, Kamath and Steinke motivate their exact sampler by noting that "seemingly innocuous numerical errors can entirely destroy privacy," which is what happened one dependency down.

glossary.definition: The parameter bounding how much any single record may change the distribution of a released answer; the mechanism promises that every output's probability moves by at most a factor of e^ε.

Adding integer-valued noise whose probability falls off geometrically with distance from zero, chosen over continuous Laplace because an integer distribution can be sampled exactly on a finite machine.
The largest integer dividing two numbers; rational arithmetic uses it to reduce fractions, and reducing by the wrong one produces a fraction that is close to the right value but not equal to it.

The log-ratio of the probabilities a mechanism assigns to the same output on two neighbouring datasets; the privacy claim is a bound on it, so reconstructing it empirically is how you test an implementation.

items.title: A GPU posts a remote write in 0.7 µs; the library adds up to 4.6 more
items.dek: Javid Baydamirli and co-authors wrote minimal GPU and CPU-proxy network transports, measured them beside NVSHMEM, NCCL GIN, DeepEP and three other libraries on H100, H200, B200 and GB200 systems, and found the bare path from a GPU thread to the network card issues a remote-memory operation in 0.7 µs.
items.why_it_matters: Mixture-of-experts inference stands on small latency-critical all-to-all messages, and the working assumption is that letting GPU threads drive the network card directly is what makes them fast. The measurement says the submission path is not what decides: queue management, memory ordering and completion scope inside the libraries add up to 4.6 µs on top of that 0.7, issue time tracks the streaming-multiprocessor clock, and sharing a queue with bulk traffic costs one to three orders of magnitude.
items.background_md: Remote direct memory access lets one machine write into another's memory without either CPU touching the payload: the sender hands the network card a work request describing the transfer, then writes to a doorbell register to say a request is waiting. Historically only a CPU thread could do that, so a GPU wanting to send had to wake a proxy thread, which costs a core and a detour through host memory. Letting the GPU's own streaming multiprocessors build the descriptor and ring the doorbell removes both, and is the premise under every modern expert-parallel communication library.
items.deeper_md:
A minimal GPU path issues in 0.7 µs and completes in 4.0 µs. The libraries measured against it — NVSHMEM IBGDA, NCCL GIN, DeepEP, UCCL-EP, MSCCL++ and fabric-lib — add as much as 4.6 µs of issue time through queue management, memory ordering and completion scope, and because the work-request construction runs on the SMs, issue time scales with the SM clock. A tuned CPU proxy matches or beats the GPU path at idle, at the price of a dedicated core whose power state then sets both its latency and its throughput.

The scaling results are the ones that bite. Sharing a queue with bulk traffic raises latency by one to three orders of magnitude. Reaching the platform's 260 M msg/s InfiniBand ceiling requires doorbell batching and queue parallelism, both of which cost resources, and all-to-all traffic gives up 59% of the NIC message rate at roughly 3,000 active connections. Merely linking communication code can cut GPU block residency even when it is never called.

This decomposes rather than disputes the original claim: NVIDIA's own introduction of GPU-initiated transfers in NVSHMEM 2.6.0 reported up to 9.5× throughput for sub-1 KiB block-puts and 180 M scalar puts per second on ConnectX-6. The limit is one InfiniBand fabric and one vendor's GPUs, so the connection-scaling number in particular is a property of that platform.

glossary.definition: A transfer where the network card reads or writes application memory on both ends without the operating system or CPU copying the data, which is what makes microsecond-scale remote access possible.
A memory-mapped register on the network card that the sender writes to announce that a new work request is queued; it is the handoff point where software stops and hardware starts.
NVIDIA's mechanism letting GPU streaming multiprocessors build network work requests and ring the doorbell themselves, replacing a CPU proxy thread that previously had to do it on the GPU's behalf.

Issue time is how long the sender spends handing the request over; completion time is how long until the transfer is acknowledged. Only the first is under the library's control, which is why separating them matters.

items.title: A looped transformer is its own weak model, so contrast the two passes
items.dek: Weihao Liu and co-authors noticed that a transformer which reruns one shared block several times already holds a weaker prediction inside it — the output of an early pass — and that subtracting that from the final pass, with no training and no second model, took Ouro-2.6B's AIME 2024 score from 61.88% to 73.33%.
items.why_it_matters: Contrastive decoding ordinarily needs two models, a strong one and a deliberately weak one, and paying to run both is why it never became standard. Recurrence hands over the pair at no cost, because the early pass is the same weights with less compute applied to them. The consequence to watch is arithmetic: guided at half the recurrent depth, these models match or exceed their own full-depth accuracy for 52–78% of the forward FLOPs.
items.background_md: A looped, or recurrent-depth, transformer gets its depth by running one block repeatedly rather than stacking distinct layers, so a three-billion-parameter model can perform the arithmetic of a much larger one by paying in passes instead of weights. Every pass leaves a hidden state that the output head could decode into a next-token distribution, and ordinary decoding discards all but the last. Separately, contrastive decoding rests on the observation that a weaker model's characteristic failures — repetition, drift, incoherence — point away from the text you actually want.
items.deeper_md:
Two variants. LoopCD-Logits decodes both the first and the final recurrent state through the output layers and combines them as `z′ = z_R + ω(z_R − z₁)`, costing one extra output pass; LoopCD-Hidden does the same subtraction on hidden states before the coda layers, `h′ = h_R + ω(h_R − h₁)`, and costs nothing extra. Guidance strength ω is fixed at 0.5 for multiple-choice scoring and 0.2–0.3 for generation, or adaptive as `ω = ω_max[1 − (p₍₁₎ − p₍₂₎)]` — push hardest exactly when the top two candidates are closest.

Tested across Ouro at 1.4B and 2.6B, Huginn 3.5B at 16 and 32 iterations, Parcae at 370M and 1.3B, and a Looped-Qwen3 4.0B built on a frozen base. Huginn's HumanEval pass@1 moves 22.56% → 31.71%.

The caveats deserve the same weight as the headline. AIME 2024 is 30 problems, so 61.88% → 73.33% is roughly three and a half questions and pass@1 on it is noisy. GSM8K improves in six of ten configurations and falls by as much as 1.29 points on Huginn at 32 iterations. And the authors say plainly that the FLOP savings are theoretical arithmetic counts, not measured wall-clock — a looped model's bottleneck is usually memory traffic per pass, which this does not change.

glossary.definition: An architecture that reuses one block for many sequential passes instead of having separate layers, so test-time compute can be dialled up without adding parameters.
The fraction of problems solved by a model's single first attempt; on a 30-problem set each problem is worth 3.3 points, which is why small benchmarks produce large-looking swings.
The coefficient multiplying the difference between the strong and weak predictions; at zero the method reduces to ordinary decoding, and too large a value amplifies noise into confident errors.
The count of floating-point operations in one forward pass, a measure of arithmetic work that ignores memory movement — which is why a FLOP saving need not be a time saving.

foundations.subtitle: A chip that moves data with light is mostly a chip that cannot make light — the standing context behind today's programmable-nonlinearity and resonator-free-memory items.
foundations.tldr: A silicon photonic chip is a set of light pipes etched into the same silicon a transistor is made from, fed by a laser that is almost always somewhere else. Silicon is very good at guiding light and bad at making it, detecting it, or switching it, and nearly every design decision in the field follows from those four facts.

sections.heading: The one thing silicon is unambiguously good at
sections.body_md:
Start with what works. Silicon sits in a cladding of its own oxide, and the refractive-index step between the two is large. A big index step means the guided mode is squeezed into a cross-section a few hundred nanometres across and can be bent around a radius of a few microns without leaking, which is the entire reason thousands of optical components fit on a die instead of on a bench.

The bill arrives as scattering. A tightly confined mode carries a large fraction of its energy right at the core boundary, so every nanometre of sidewall roughness the etch leaves behind couples light out, and that — not absorption in the silicon — is what sets the loss of a conventional single-mode guide. Widen the core until it is formally multimode and keep the fundamental mode away from the walls, and the loss falls to about 0.1 dB/cm with no special processing at all. A racetrack resonator built that way on a stock 220 nm silicon-on-insulator shuttle process reached an intrinsic Q of 1.02 × 10⁷, equivalent to 0.065 dB/cm, and a 100 cm on-chip delay line measured about 0.14 dB/cm.
sections.deeper_md: The comparison that makes the trade legible is silicon nitride, which has a smaller index step and therefore a less tightly confined mode. Wafer-scale nitride circuits reach a mean Q above 30 million, a propagation loss of 1.0 dB/m — two orders of magnitude better than silicon — and a metre of spiral waveguide fits in a 5 × 5 mm die at 2.4 dB/m. The absorption-limited Q of those resonators exceeds a billion, which says the remaining loss is scattering and interface chemistry, not the material. What nitride gives up is bend radius and the ability to host a free-carrier modulator at all, which is why real platforms ship both and route between them.

sections.heading: Silicon cannot emit light, and that is band structure, not engineering
sections.body_md:
A semiconductor emits light efficiently when an electron at the bottom of the conduction band can drop into a hole at the top of the valence band without changing momentum. In silicon those two extrema sit at different points in momentum space, so the transition needs a phonon to carry the difference — a three-body event, far less likely than the two-body one. Cubic silicon, germanium and all their alloys are indirect in exactly this way and cannot emit light efficiently; the point was sharpened recently by growing the same atoms in a hexagonal lattice instead, which *is* direct and shows a subnanosecond radiative lifetime and a yield comparable to III-V semiconductors.

So the laser comes from elsewhere. In practice that means indium phosphide or gallium arsenide, either packaged off-chip and coupled in through a vertical grating or an edge coupler, or bonded or grown onto the silicon afterwards. This is the single structural fact that shapes silicon photonics economics: the thing generating every photon on the chip was not made by the process that made the chip, and alignment, thermal budget and yield all follow from that.

sections.heading: Modulation: no Pockels effect, so push carriers around
sections.body_md:
Silicon's crystal has a centre of inversion, and a centrosymmetric material has no linear electro-optic effect — no Pockels coefficient, which is the mechanism lithium niobate modulators use. The available knob is the free-carrier plasma effect: inject or remove electrons and holes from the waveguide and the refractive index moves a little.

The two ways of doing it trade against each other cleanly. Carrier injection, forward-biasing a diode across the guide, gives a large index change but has the junction capacitance and minority-carrier lifetime of a forward-biased diode, so it is slow. Carrier depletion, reverse-biasing instead, has much lower junction capacitance and therefore far higher electro-optic bandwidth, but the index change is small. A recent design study makes the dependence on geometry concrete: depletion-mode Mach-Zehnder modulators on thick 5 µm and 3 µm silicon-on-insulator — which tolerate fabrication spread and handle optical power well — reach a few gigabits per second, while the same design on a 220 nm device layer reaches 20 Gb/s. A small index change means either a long arm or a resonator, and that choice is where wavelength sensitivity enters the design.
sections.deeper_md: The absence of a native χ⁽²⁾ is not necessarily permanent, and the workaround is instructive. Apply a static bias to a material with a third-order nonlinearity and you synthesise an effective second-order one, χ⁽²⁾ = 3χ⁽³⁾E_bias — the electric-field-induced second-harmonic route. In a silicon-nitride waveguide driven at 800 V AC, that yields roughly 0.29 pm/V, which is weak against a poled ferroelectric but is spatially patternable, since the field pattern can be set by shining light on a photoconductive electrode rather than by a fixed metal geometry.

sections.heading: Germanium does the detecting, for the same reason silicon guides
sections.body_md:
The property that makes silicon a good waveguide at 1310 nm and 1550 nm is that it does not absorb there — the photon energy is below its band gap. The same property disqualifies it as the detector. A material that absorbs the light you are carrying is a material that would have attenuated it on the way.

The standard answer is germanium, which absorbs across both telecom bands and, being a group IV element, can be grown epitaxially on silicon in the same fab. Every serious platform therefore ships a germanium epilayer photodiode as a library component — GlobalFoundries' photonic process design kit lists exactly that alongside its nitride waveguides, modulators, phase shifters, polarisation splitter-rotators and vertical grating incouplers. The germanium is not free: its lattice constant does not match silicon's, so the epitaxy relieves the mismatch by making threading dislocations, and dislocations are leakage, which is dark current, which is detector noise. Selective growth in windows, buffer layers and post-growth anneals are all about keeping that defect density down, and they are why the photodiode is a foundry-qualified block rather than something a designer draws.

sections.heading: What a foundry actually hands you
sections.body_md:
Here is the thing that separates silicon photonics from most research optics: you can buy it. GlobalFoundries' 45SPCLO is a 45 nm generation silicon-on-insulator CMOS process with the photonics integrated monolithically, run on 300 mm wafers at Fab 8 in Malta, New York. The kit contains C-band and O-band transceiver blocks, modulators, detectors, phase shifters, polarisation splitter-rotators, vertical grating incouplers, germanium epilayer photodiodes and nitride waveguides — and, on the same masks, several flavours of FET including analog and thick-oxide devices, precision resistors and decoupling capacitors.

Monolithic is the word that matters. The transistor driving a modulator and the modulator itself share a mask set: no microbump, no bond wire, no separate electronic die, and therefore a driver-to-device parasitic set by layout rather than by packaging. The price is the node. You get photonics on a 45 nm logic process, not a leading-edge one, because the photonic layers and the thermal budget they need do not survive a modern transistor flow. Access is through multi-project shuttles: a 5 × 5 mm block, about 50 dies back, five to six months of turnaround.
sections.deeper_md: The shuttle numbers are worth sitting with, because they set what kind of experiment is possible. One 25 mm² block, 50 dies, two runs a year. That is a design-of-experiments budget, not an iteration budget: you cannot afford to find out which of six waveguide widths works by trying six waveguide widths on successive tapeouts. It is the same arithmetic that makes mask cost the governing constraint on student silicon generally, and it is why so much of this field's effort goes into either simulation fidelity or post-fabrication programmability.

sections.heading: Where the tolerance lands, and the two live answers
sections.body_md:
Collect the constraints and one failure mode dominates everything. Index contrast is high, so the propagating phase depends steeply on the waveguide's cross-section; the cross-section is set by lithography and etch; and the device is centimetres long. A nanometre-scale width variation that no process controls perfectly becomes an accumulated phase error that no designer specified. For a resonant device it shows up as a resonance landing somewhere other than where it was drawn, which is why every microring in a shipping product is paired with a heater and a control loop, and why a resonant photonic memory has never scaled into an array.

There are three answers in play, and they are worth recognising as the same answer attacked from different sides. Make the mode less sensitive to the sidewall, which is what the broadened multimode cores do. Make the phase profile programmable after fabrication, which is what writing a quasi-phase-matching grating with projected light does. Or refuse to use a resonance at all, which is what building a memory cell from broadband attenuators does. Each one accepts a worse nominal number to get a number that survives manufacturing.

glossary.definition: A wafer with a thin single-crystal silicon device layer sitting on buried oxide. In photonics the oxide is the lower cladding and the device-layer thickness — 220 nm is the common choice — fixes the mode shape and therefore every design rule above it.

Propagation loss per centimetre of waveguide, on a logarithmic scale: 3 dB/cm halves the power every centimetre, 0.1 dB/cm costs about 2.3% per centimetre. It is the number that decides whether a long delay line or a large interferometer is buildable.

A shallow periodic corrugation etched into the waveguide that diffracts light up out of the chip plane, so a fibre can be brought in from above. It is the usual route for getting light from an off-chip laser onto the die, and it is wavelength- and polarisation-selective.

A refractive-index change proportional to applied electric field. It requires a material with no centre of inversion, which silicon has, so silicon modulators cannot use it and must move free carriers instead.

A run in which many customers' designs share one mask set and one wafer lot, splitting the mask cost. It is what makes a foundry process reachable by a university group, and its block size and cadence set the pace of any academic photonics project.

An interferometer that splits light into two arms, shifts the phase in one of them electrically, and recombines — converting a phase change into an intensity change. Unlike a ring resonator it is broadband, so it needs no wavelength tuning, at the cost of a much longer device.

foundations.try_this: Install KLayout and add SiEPIC-Tools, both free, and open the bundled Generic Silicon Photonics kit. Lay out a Mach-Zehnder with two unequal arms, run the layout verification and netlist extraction, and watch it flag the places where your waveguide is not actually connected to what you thought. Then read the abstract and Fig. 1 of Zhang et al., arXiv:2104.04239, and work out why their deliberately multimode broadened core has lower loss than the single-mode waveguide you just drew — the answer is where the mode's energy sits relative to the etched sidewall, and it is the single most useful intuition in the field. UMN's library subscription also reaches the paywalled 2016 Journal of Optics silicon-photonics roadmap if you want the long version.
